NEW DELHI: India on Wednesday condemned strikes by Iran-backed Houthis on Saudi Arabian oil and civilian facilities, saying that such attacks undermine regional security."India condemns attacks on Saudi sovereign territory, especially the targeting of civilian and economic facilities. Attacks that undermine regional security and stability and threaten freedom of navigation in the Bab-el-Mandeb were unacceptable," ministry of external affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said in response to a media query.Jaiswal’s remarks came as the Houthis, the Yemen-based rebel group, targeted Saudi oil facilities and other civilian infrastructure on Tuesday, raising widespread concerns over a further escalation of the conflict in the Middle East.The attacks on Saudi Arabia came as the US intensified its economic sanctions against Iran.As many as 73 people were wounded in a wave of Houthi attacks that targeted “civilian and economic facilities” in the Saudi Arabian cities of Abha, Jazan, Najran and Khamis Mushait.The strikes came hours after the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out an air strike on a prison in Yemen’s northern Jawf province. At least seven people, including a child, were killed and seven others wounded in the strike in the city of Hazem.Yemen’s civil war began in 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa, along with large parts of northern Yemen, forcing the internationally recognised government into exile.A Saudi-led coalition, which included the United Arab Emirates, intervened the following year in an effort to restore the government to power.Tensions between the US allies Saudi Arabia and the UAE escalated earlier this year as their partnership in Yemen’s war deteriorated, ultimately prompting the UAE to withdraw from the conflict.The civil war has killed at least 150,000 people, according to UN estimates, and at times pushed Yemen to the brink of famine.

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian president Vladimir Putin are scheduled to hold a bilateral meeting on Friday, with trade and economic cooperation expected to feature prominently on the agenda, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said.Moscow also welcomed India’s willingness to contribute to efforts aimed at finding a peaceful resolution to the Ukraine conflict.Putin is scheduled to visit India for the BRICS Summit, which will begin in New Delhi on September 12. Ahead of the visit, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said the trip will provide an opportunity for the two countries to discuss issues concerning bilateral relations. He also wished India success in hosting the summit."In a couple of days, President Putin will begin his India visit. You know that our two leaders, Indian and Russian leaders, are in a very close personal contact. They are very pragmatic in their relationship, and they are as sincere as to be able to discuss in a very open and constructive way the most sensitive issues of our agenda and our bilateral relations. Of course, it opens additional horizons for our cooperation," Peskov said."We have no doubt that the summit will be successful. Russia, we are doing our best to contribute to further development of BRICS cooperation in the three main pillars of our interaction. So, those are policy and security. economy and finance, and cultural and humanitarian contexts. So, we are supporting idea of inviting new countries to join different formats within BRICS," he added.Peskov said Russia is awaiting negotiations with India on setting up new nuclear power plants, adding that the sale of Su-57 fighter aircraft to India is also on the agenda.The Kremlin spokesperson stressed the need for cooperation in the financial sector, alleging that some countries were using their currencies as a tool of political oppression."The cooperation space within Brics financial sphere is of great importance. Russia recently reached a level of 90 percent of all the payments, all the transactions with Brics countries being made in national currencies, it's very important. It's not because we are aiming for de-dollarization, for getting rid of US dollars. To the contrary, we are open to to every acceptable methods of payments, but you know that certain countries are using some national currencies as a tool for political oppression.They are introducing sanctions based on their national currencies. So, if they don't let us use their money, we use our own money," Peskov said.India is set to host the 18th Brics Summit in New Delhi on September 12-13, 2026, as the grouping of major emerging market economies and developing nations continues to expand its role in global affairs.The grouping began as Bric, comprising Brazil, Russia, India and China. It held its first Foreign Ministers’ meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York in 2006, followed by its inaugural summit in Yekaterinburg, Russia, in 2009. South Africa joined the grouping in 2011, leading to the formation of BRICS.Under India’s 2026 chairship theme, “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability,” New Delhi is seeking to move the grouping’s agenda beyond political coordination towards practical cooperation in areas including trade, agriculture, healthcare, energy, digital technology, urban development, small enterprises, startups, climate action and cultural exchanges.
Article Summary: Pm modi and russian president vladimir putin are scheduled to hold a bilateral meeting on friday. Trade and economic cooperation expected to feature prominently on the agenda. Putin is scheduled to visit india for the brics summit, which will begin in new delhi on september 12.

Article Title: UPI-ng the ante: PM Modi wants desi connect with global pay
Article Text:
PM wants desi connect with global pay

MUMBAI: PM Narendra Modi Tuesday called for India to set its own standards and protocols for cross-border payments and directly integrate its payment system with countries where Indian diaspora populations are large and trade volumes significant.He said India now had a sovereign alternative to the foreign standards under-pinning the existing card-payment architecture and could connect it with the global financial system.Modi said the move could also reduce the cost of remittances, noting that Indians abroad send the largest volume of money home globally but lose a notable portion to transaction fees. “UPI can deliver substantial savings here as well, allowing funds to reach Indian families far more rapidly,” he said.His remarks came ahead of the Brics summit, where expanding national and local currency trade is a priority. A proposal seeks to enable retail and trade-settlement interoperability between fast-payment systems by linking UPI with similar networks in other countries. India has been looking at ways to reduce reliance on the dollar for cross-currency trade while Brics has stopped short of referring to the dollar, with the 2025 declaration calling for finding “acceptable mechanisms of financing in local currencies”.“We have already accomplished this with Singapore. As a result, cross-border transactions between India and Singapore occur as seamlessly as transfers between two neighbourhoods of the same city. We must replicate these integrations across other countries and international markets,” the PM said.Addressing Global Fintech Fest for the third consecutive year, Modi said India had gr-own 7.8% despite pressure on energy and commodity supply chains and escalating trade tensions. He also cited a Japanese ratings agency upgrading India to the A category, a milestone achieved after three decades. “This reflects how confident the world has become in the structural reforms implemented over the past years. And I reiterate: India’s ‘Reform Express’ will advance at an even faster pace,” he said.The PM called for stronger cybersecurity, industry-led ethical data-protection stand-ards, a regulatory-industry innovation ecosystem and a fintech consumer-protection index with clear and transparent ratings. He also said the sector needed to diversify beyond payments by expanding credit, insurance, savings, investments and pension products.Noting that Global Fintech Fest coincided with UPI’s 10th anniversary, Modi said those excluded from formal banking for generations were now driving fintech growth.He said SVANidhi credit cards had brought street vendors into the formal credit system by giving them a verifiable tool for access. Studies, he said, showed average annual income among PM SVANidhi beneficiaries had risen by over 20%.Noting that besides fintech energy, Mumbai’s cultural energy was also at its peak thanks to Ganeshotsav festivities around the corner, Modi extended warm wishes. Attending the annual fest for the third consecutive time, Modi said, would be his second “hat trick” — the first being in 2024 when NDA formed govt for a third time.
Article Summary: Pm narendra modi calls for india to set its own standards and protocols for cross-border payments. He said india now had a sovereign alternative to the foreign standards under-pinning the existing card-payment architecture. His remarks came ahead of the brics summit, where expanding national and local currency trade is a priority.

Article Title: Indians trust the classroom, see better opportunities abroad: Global survey
Article Text:
File Image

Phir Bhi Dil Hai Hindustani.

The robust belief in education, with a rider

Education confidence chart

Optimism about Yuva Shakti

Highest youth optimism score

The Indian dream remains intergenerational

India's faith on future

In India, the college degree has not lost its promise

Reimagining Skilling

for Viksit Bharat@2047

Bullish on college degree

India trusts the curriculum, yet worries about the jobs connection

Education-Jobs paradox

A bright future. Somewhere else?

Hope at home, opportunity abroad

Social media? Restrict it. AI? Not necessarily

On use of AI

Not because the Ipsos Education Monitor survey mirrors the plot of the Shah Rukh Khan-Juhi Chawla film, but because the title neatly captures the contradiction in its India findings. Indians may believe better opportunities for growth and prosperity lie offshore, yet they remain remarkably bullish about their education system, their degrees and, above all, the future of their youth.More than half of Indian respondents rate the country’s education system as good. Three-fourths believe youth will have a better life than their parents. Nearly two-thirds think even young people from lesser privileged backgrounds have a bright future. And Indians remain strikingly convinced that a university degree still has value. However, ironically, 76% of Indian respondents say young people would have better opportunities by moving abroad.For some parameters, TOI looked at the subset of India’s position among the 16 individual G20 member countries included in the 31-country Ipsos survey. China, Russia and Saudi Arabia were not surveyed. The survey covered 23,537 online adults across the 31 countries between June and July 2026, with about 1,000 respondents in India.Ipsos in its methodology has cautioned that its India sample is more urban, educated and/or affluent than the general population and should be interpreted as reflecting the views of the country’s more “connected” segment.The 31-country average is an unweighted average of country results; it is not adjusted for the population size of each country.The first question was straightforward. How do people rate the overall quality of their country’s education system? In India, 51% called it good. Among the G20 countries covered by the survey, only Australia was higher, at 53%. The 31-country average was 33%. But that 51% is a number in retreat. India was at 65% in 2025, 69% in 2024 and 55% in 2023. The 14-point fall from 2025 is the steepest year-on-year decline among countries with comparable 2025 data.The contrast with several richer economies is sharp. Britain was at 43%, the US and Brazil at 32%, Italy at 29%, Japan at 24%, while France and Germany were both at 17%. That does not mean India has a better-performing education system than advanced economies. This is a matter of perception. And on that measure, Indians appear unusually confident. Just less than before.The gap becomes even more striking when the question shifts from institutions to the people coming out of them. Asked whether young people in their country have a bright future, 72% of Indian respondents agreed. That was not merely the highest figure among the G20 countries covered. It was the highest among all 31 countries surveyed. The 31-country average was 45%.Within the surveyed G20 set, Australia and South Africa were next at 54%, followed by Mexico at 52% and Canada at 50%. France was at 22%. It is perhaps one of the strongest votes of confidence in the survey. Indians appear to have placed enormous hope in their youth to put the country on the right track and take it forward.One of the hallmarks of an aspirational society like India is the belief in accumulating wealth and opportunity across generations. People believe that the hard work of one generation will make the lives of those that follow smoother. That belief gets backed in this survey. Three-fourths of Indian respondents, 75%, believe young people today will have a better life than their parents. The 31-country average is 48%.Indians are also optimistic about people escaping the poverty trap. 64% believe young people from poorer backgrounds have a bright future, compared with a 31-country average of 40%. India is the highest among the G20 countries covered on both measures. And 69% of Indian respondents believe the education system contributes to reducing social inequalities, again the highest among the surveyed G20 countries. That figure is also below earlier readings, 72% in 2024 and 79% in 2023.Together, these numbers suggest that Indian respondents continue to see education as a vehicle for upward social mobility. That belief becomes even clearer when the survey turns to higher education. NITI Aayog ’s recent report also points to the continuing pull of degree programmes, noting that vocational pathways are often not seen as credible, growth-oriented alternatives and that degrees can become the safer choice amid limited counselling, social bias and low trust in existing skill systems. The Ipsos survey, albeit with a more urban and connected Indian sample, points in a similar direction. 75% of Indian respondents say a college or university degree is very important to succeed in life. 78% believe it helps people go further in their careers. And 70% say degrees in their country offer good value for money.On the first measure, India is the highest among the G20 countries surveyed. On both the other measures, it ranks second. The contrast with several advanced economies is large. On whether a degree is good value for money, India’s 70% compares with 38% in the US, 41% in Germany, 30% in Japan and 28% in Britain. Ipsos itself finds a strong positive relationship across countries between believing that a degree helps a career and believing that it offers value for money.Here again, the Ipsos study broadly aligns with a concern flagged in NITI Aayog’s skilling report that education and credentials do not automatically translate into the skills and pathways that the labour market demands. The Ipsos survey shows a deep-seated faith in formal education and yet a growing realisation that job-market demands are at times different from what is being taught in the classroom.Asked whether the school curriculum adequately prepares students for future careers, 67% of Indians agree, the highest share among the G20 countries covered by the survey. Even here, the direction has been downward: 74% agreed in 2024, 72% in 2025 and 67% now.Yet in another question on the greatest challenges facing young people, 36% of Indian respondents select “education and training systems not matching labour market demands”. That too is the highest among the G20 countries in the survey.India again falls on one extreme of a scatter plot for its two seemingly contradictory sets of beliefs. On one hand, 72% say young people have a bright future. On the other hand, 76% say young people would have better opportunities by moving abroad. The 31-country average on that question is 62%.Indonesia and South Africa are even more likely to say opportunities are better overseas, at 87% and 80% respectively. Italy is at 79%. Romania matches India at 76%. But none combines that level of outward-looking aspiration with India’s exceptional optimism about the future of its young.This is perhaps the central finding of the entire report for India. Respondents may be optimistic about India’s young people precisely because they believe those young people possess education and skills that give them more options, including the option of leaving. The optimism may be about the people. The doubt may be about the location of opportunity.The dichotomy in the approach of Indians extends to technology too. 78% support banning social media for children under 14, both inside and outside school. The 31-country average is 73%.Support has climbed 10 points in a year. India was at 68% in 2025 and 73% in 2024.On smartphones, 57% of Indian respondents favour a ban in schools, exactly matching the 31-country average. That is up from 50% last year and 52% in 2024. But attitudes to AI are different.Only 26% of Indian respondents say AI, including ChatGPT, should be banned in schools, compared with 39% across the 31 countries. Indian opinion on AI has moved sharply over the four editions of the survey. 39% wanted AI banned in schools in both 2025 and 2024, compared with just 16% in 2023. The 13-point drop from 2025 to 2026 is the largest year-on-year fall among countries with comparable 2025 data.Britain, the US and Poland moved in the other direction, rising to 52%, 56% and 46%, respectively.To sum up, India’s ‘connected’ population has not lost faith in education. Quite the opposite. It remains unusually convinced that education matters, degrees pay, children can surpass their parents and those from poorer homes can climb. What appears less certain is where that promise will ultimately be realised.andmay finally be different. That is the sobering realisation one can derive from this survey.
Article Summary: More than half of indian respondents rate the country’s education system as good. Three-fourths believe youth will have a better life than their parents. Nearly two-thirds think even young people from lesser privileged backgrounds have a bright future. Three-fourths of indian respondents, 75%, believe young people today will have a better life than their parents.

Article Title: India, China hold first high-level military flag talks in Arunachal amid LAC tensions
Article Text:
India, China hold first high-level military flag meeting in Arunachal sector

New military mechanism along eastern frontier

Border peace remains key to improving ties

Military engagement ahead of Xi visit

NEW DELHI: India and China have held their first Senior Highest Military Commander-Level Flag Meeting in the Arunachal Pradesh sector, with talks taking place on both sides of the frontier earlier this week.The meeting followed understandings reached during the Special Representatives dialogue between National Security Advisor (NSA) Ajit Doval and Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi. The talks are part of efforts by the two countries to maintain peace along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) and gradually improve bilateral ties.MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said the meeting was held at Wacha on the Indian side on September 6 and at Damai on the Chinese side on September 7.Jaiswal said the meeting followed agreements reached during the Special Representatives talks in August 2025 and August 2026, along with subsequent discussions under the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination."Pursuant to the understandings reached between the Special Representatives of India and China in August 2025 and August 2026, and subsequent discussions at the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination meetings held in Beijing and New Delhi in May and August 2026 respectively, the first Senior Highest Military Commander-Level Flag Meeting was held at Wacha on the Indian side in Arunachal Pradesh on September 6 and Damai on the Chinese side on September 7," Jaiswal said at his weekly media briefing."A similar mechanism also exists in the Western Sector," he said.The talks took place amid reports of aggressive military posturing by Chinese troops along the LAC in the Upper Subansiri region of Arunachal Pradesh.Jaiswal also said that India-China relations are gradually moving in a "positive direction".Doval and Wang, who are the designated Special Representatives for the India-China boundary talks, held their latest dialogue in Beijing last month.During the meeting, the two sides discussed the delimitation of the boundary, trans-boundary cooperation and the need to maintain peace along the LAC.The Indian side stressed that peace and tranquillity along the border are important for the continued development of bilateral relations.The Special Representatives mechanism was established in 2003 to address the India-China boundary dispute, which covers a 3,488-km frontier.India and China have taken several steps in recent months to rebuild relations that deteriorated sharply after the deadly Galwan Valley clashes in 2020. The latest military engagement comes days before Chinese president Xi Jinping is expected to visit India for the BRICS summit. Xi is likely to arrive in New Delhi on Saturday.
Article Summary: India, china hold first high-level military flag meeting in arunachal sector. Talks are part of efforts by the two countries to maintain peace along the line of actual control (lac) the latest military engagement comes days before chinese president xi jinping is expected to visit india for the brics summit.

Article Title: Putin meeting PM Modi on Friday; energy, defence high on agenda

Energy and defence high on agenda

India & Russia exploring cooperation on rare earths

Russia described as illegal and unacceptable the US move to impose 100% tariffs on nations importing Russian oil, while confirming another bilateral meeting between PM Modi and President Vladimir Putin on Friday. Putin is travelling to India this week for his first overseas participation in a BRICS summit since the Russia-Ukraine war started in Feb 2022.Ahead of the visit, a Kremlin spokesperson said India’s energy imports from Russia were setting new records and both countries also had similar positions on the war. He welcomed India’s intention to facilitate a peaceful resolution of the conflict.India will host the BRICS summit on Sept 12-13. While China is yet to officially confirm President Xi Jinping’s participation, diplomatic sour­ces said he’s likely to arrive Saturday and have a bilateral meet with Modi the same day.Modi and Putin had met on Aug 31 on the margins of the SCO summit in Bishkek. In their bilateral meeting Friday, the two will look to ramp up trade, energy and defence ties. Dmitry Peskov, the Russian presidential spokesperson, said that both sides are exploring cooperation on rare earths and also the sale of Sukhoi Su-57 stealth fighter jets to India.Against the backdrop of Modi’s message to Putin that it was high time the “endless” war was brought to an end, the official said India’s position on Ukraine was aligned with Moscow’s stand.“We know India’s position on the Ukrainian conflict, and to a great extent... it corresponds with our own position, because we do want the resolution of the Ukrainian conflict by peaceful means, and Russia is open to this process,” Peskov said.He denied that Brics was considering de-dollarisation but said certain countries were using their national currencies as tools of political oppression and called the proposed US sanctions illegal and unacceptable.Committing to further expanding energy cooperation with India, the official said India’s energy imports from Russia are at a record high. “I don’t want to give you any figures for understandable reasons, but every month we have a new record,” he said, briefing journalists virtually ahead of Putin’s visit.The official also said that delivery of Russia’s S-400 Triumf air defence systems to India in 2026 was also on the agenda. “Russia is capable of fulfilling its obligations, and they will be fulfilled. This issue is being mentioned during the conversations of our two leaders,” said Peskov.

Article Title: Meta India officials summoned over child abuse ads
Article Text:
Meta India officials summoned over child abuse ads

NEW DELHI: National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) has summoned Meta India's managing director and country head to appear before it on Wednesday over advertisements allegedly linked to child sexual exploitation and abuse material (CSEAM) on Instagram.NCPCR commission took suo motu cognisance of a BBC Eye report and issued a notice to Meta Platforms Inc on July 3, seeking an explanation and documents. Meta replied a week later, following which the NCPCR instituted a formal inquiry to establish the facts.Commission officials remained tight-lipped about Meta's response. However, they said the inquiry would examine Meta India's role in the appearance of the advertisements, how they cleared Instagram's systems and why the situation arose.The scrutiny would consider the stringent provisions relating to such material under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, they added.Last week, NHRC issued notices to the ministry of electronics and information technology and ministry of information and broadcasting as part of its scrutiny of alleged CSAM on Instagram. An NHRC member Priyank Kanoongo, whose bench issued the notices Sept 2, said the inquiry was no longer only identifying who uploaded the content. "It also examines the extent to which the platform's own editorial and publishing systems participate in the generation, selection, circulation, amplification or monetisation of content," he said. The company denied knowingly targeting such advertisements at people.Queries to Meta did not elicit a response.
Article Summary: Meta india officials summoned over child abuse ads on instagram. National commission for protection of child rights (ncpcr) took suo motu cognisance of a bbc eye report and issued a notice to meta platforms inc. The company denied knowingly targeting such advertisements at people.

Article Title: Sri Lanka a close friend, India stands by it: Rajnath Singh
Article Text:

Defence minister Rajnath Singh said in Colombo Tuesday that India and Sri Lanka are close friends and India will always stand firmly with Sri Lanka whenever the island nation faces a crisis.Singh, who is on a three-day visit to Sri Lanka, has become the first Indian defence minister to visit the island nation for defence-level talks after nearly 40 years. KC Pant was the defence minister to visit the island for such talks in 1988. "The relationship between India and Sri Lanka is based on shared history, culture, and faith. We stand with Sri Lanka through thick and thin and are committed to the peace, prosperity, and development of both countries," said Singh as he began his visit with an interaction with the Indian diaspora.Singh said both nations share close cultural and civilisational ties which have provided a strong foundation for the growth of bilateral relationship. "I am experiencing a sense of belonging after coming here," he said while emphasising the importance of robust regional alliances. He highlighted India's expanding global influence and economic strength, and appreciated the work done by the diaspora.Before leaving for Colombo, Rajnath posted on X, "Besides our longstanding partnership as well as deep historical and civilisational ties, Sri Lanka is one of our most important partners under the 'Neighbourhood First' and 'MAHASAGAR' initiatives."Addressing the diaspora, Rajnath highlighted India's rapid economic transformation, stating that the country is among the fastest-growing major economies in the world and contributes more than 16% to global growth.He said that India's economy, which stood at $2 trillion in 2014, has doubled to approximately $4 trillion over the last decade.The defence minister added that amid global economic challenges, the country's economy grew at 7.8% in the first quarter of financial year 2026-27. Singh also underlined the improvement in macroeconomic stability, saying that average inflation over the last 12 years has been approximately 4.7%, compared to 10-11% during the earlier period.The minister said India has concluded trade deals with 38 countries over the last 12 years, including free trade agreements with eight major nations, compared to just four before 2014.Referring to the India-EU FTA as the 'Mother of all deals', he said the agreement opens access to the massive EU market and reflects India's growing diplomatic and economic capabilities.
Article Summary: Sri lanka a close friend, india stands by it: rajnath singh. Singh has become the first indian defence minister to visit the island nation for defence-level talks after nearly 40 years. He highlighted india's expanding global influence and economic strength.

Article Title: Strategic autonomy in motion as India hosts Brics summit
Article Text:
Strategic autonomy in motion as India hosts Brics summit

India for Brics

Key challenges for India

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India will host the annual Brics summit on Sept 12-13 at Bharat Mandapam, returning to the venue where it held the G20 summit in 2023. That gathering is remembered for the inclusion of the African Union in G20, marking a major step in efforts to bridge the gap between the western-led global order and the emerging Global South. At Brics, India will look to leverage that momentum, working with major emerging economies to demand structural reforms of global governance institutions dominated by the West.This would be the 18th summit of the grouping that brings together 11 major emerging and developing economies - Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Ethiopia, the UAE, Indonesia, Iran, Egypt and Saudi Arabia - along with 10 other partner countries.The theme of India's 2026 chairship is 'Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability', drawing inspiration from PM Narendra Modi's 'humanity first' and people-centric approach to Brics. Under its chairship, India has so far held over 350 meetings - 25 at the ministerial level, including the foreign ministers' and national security advisers' engagements.Despite political fragmentation and economic imbalances, Brics remains important for India for multiple reasons, especially in an increasingly uncertain world.It reinforces India's strategic autonomy and multi-alignment policy, not allowing any one single bloc to acquire excessive leverage over it. That it can simultaneously expand its strategic and technology ties with the West and also work with Quad for a free and open Indo-Pacific reaffirms an independent foreign policy.Brics also allows India to showcase its Global South leadership credentials, as it works with other major emerging markets to push for reforms of global institutions like UNSC, IMF and World Bank that are not representative of the developing world. Support for UNSC reforms is important, although it falls short of an explicit endorsement of India's permanent membership bid, mainly because of China's presence.India's approach to Brics is also guided by its complex ties with China. Turning away would mean allowing China to shape the agenda of the developing world. India's moderating influence prevents the bloc from turning into an anti-West platform.There's focus too on expanding financial architecture, as no govt would like its trade to be held hostage by instruments it cannot control. As foreign minister S Jaishankar has underlined, institutions such as New Development Bank and Contingent Reserve Arrangement demonstrate the group's ability to create credible alternatives. For India, these are not initiatives targeted at any currency.Brics also provides India with markets, along with trade diversification, de-risking and supply-chain opportunities. Brics' membership deepens India's trade ties with Russia (energy), Brazil (agriculture/commodities), Gulf and African countries, diversifying away from over-reliance on any single partner.The first, of course, is to forge a consensus on West Asia that would enable a joint Brics declaration, a task complicated by the presence of the UAE and Iran in the group. India will likely focus on drafting a resolution rooted in the UN Charter, dialogue and diplomacy, freedom of navigation and civilian protection, while looking to ring-fence economic agreements from contentious political issues by acknowledging respective national positions.Balancing relations with the US is another key concern for India, which is hosting the summit fresh off a tariff firestorm with Washington. US President Donald Trump sees the grouping itself as an assault on US currency. India backs legitimate local-currency settlement while maintaining it is against any common Brics currency or China-centred replacement mechanism.Another challenge for India is to prevent China's predominance without destabilising its bilateral relations with Beijing. For all the talk about Brics' combined power, China enjoys a vastly asymmetrical influence with its trade, investment, manufacturing and critical mineral leverage. Wary of China's economic agenda, India avoided endorsing SCO's 2030 economic roadmap, and it must work with Beijing in Brics on shared objectives, though without letting the forum become a Chinese economic or geopolitical platform.This also intersects with the challenge of ensuring that an expanded grouping remains governable and cohesive, especially with countries like Pakistan and Bangladesh pursuing membership with support from Beijing.Jaishankar said while announcing the summit that Brics must transition now from a forum for discussions to a platform for delivery. In that spirit, India seems focused on delivering an outcome-oriented summit, with key deliverables like a unanimous Brics declaration, logistics supply-chain cooperation framework, incubator/startup network, development finance, cross-border payment and continued support for Indian priorities like UNSC reforms and counterterrorism.To conclude, inclusion of African Union was not the only major takeaway from 2023's G20 summit. Perhaps more dramatic was the last-minute consensus on Ukraine through a compromise language crafted by India, which allowed a G20 declaration. India can derive confidence from that diplomatic triumph as it heads into another tough but potentially rewarding global summit.

NEW DELHI: The first-ever Corps Commander–level meeting between India and China in the eastern sector was a two-day engagement, marking a milestone in bilateral efforts to maintain peace along the Line of Actual Control (LAC).“The first highest military Corps Commander–level flag meeting took place on Sept 6 at Wacha on the Indian side in Arunachal Pradesh and then the second meet happened at Damai on the Chinese side on Sept 7,” MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said. Article Title: Strategic Autonomy in motion as India hosts 18th BRICS Summit
Article Text:
This would be the 18th summit of the grouping. (Photo: ANI)

India for BRICS

Key Challenges for India

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India will host the annual BRICS summit on September 12-13 at Bharat Mandapam, returning to the venue where it held the G20 summit in 2023. That gathering is remembered for the inclusion of the African Union in G20, marking a major step in efforts to bridge the gap between the Western-led global order and the emerging Global South. At BRICS, India will look to leverage that momentum, working with major emerging economies to demand structural reforms of global governance institutions dominated by the West.This would be the 18th summit of the grouping that brings together 11 major emerging and developing economies – Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Ethiopia, UAE, Indonesia, Iran, Egypt and Saudi Arabia – along with 10 other partner countries. Together, BRICS nations account for 49 percent of world population, 40 percent of global GDP and 26 percent of international trade.The last time India hosted an in-person BRICS summit was in 2016 in Goa. This year also marks 2 decades of formalisation of the bloc for cooperation on issues related to global economic and political governance. The theme of India's 2026 chairship is Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability, drawing inspiration from PM Narendra Modi's 'humanity first' and people-centric approach to BRICS.This will also be the first summit to see in-person participation by Russian President Vladimir Putin since the start of the Ukraine war. Chinese President Xi Jinping is also visiting India for the first time in 7 years to participate in the summit.Under its chairship, India has so far held over 350 meetings - 25 at the ministerial level including the foreign ministers and national security advisers’ engagements. The ministerial meetings have so far resulted in key outcomes and initiatives spanning agriculture, health, energy, environment, disaster management and also trade, reaffirming commitment to a fair, inclusive and transparent multilateral trading system with WTO at its core.Despite the political fragmentation and economic imbalances associated with the grouping, BRICS remains important for India for multiple reasons, especially in an increasingly uncertain world. For one, it lends India a platform to practice its strategic autonomy and multi-alignment policy, not allowing any one single bloc to acquire excessive leverage over it. That it can simultaneously expand its strategic and technology ties with the West and also work with Quad for a free and open Indo-Pacific reinforces an independent foreign policy. For India, as external affairs minister S Jaishankar has said, BRICS is an embodiment of a multipolar world. India is not giving up on its Western partnerships, only hedging against uncertainty whether from US unpredictability or Chinese ascendancy.BRICS also allows India to showcase its Global South leadership credentials, as it works with other major emerging markets to push for reforms of global institutions like the UNSC, IMF and World Bank that are not representative of the developing world. Support for UNSC reforms is important, although it still falls short of an explicit endorsement of India's permanent membership bid, mainly because of China's presence.India's approach to BRICS is also guided by its complex ties with China. Turning away would mean allowing China to single-handedly shape the agenda of the developing world. BRICS is consensus driven and even for Washington and other Western capitals, India's moderating influence should be of significance as it prevents the bloc from turning into an anti-West platform.There's focus as well on expanding financial architecture as no government would like its trade to be held hostage by instruments it can't control. As Jaishankar has underlined, institutions such as the New Development Bank and the Contingent Reserve Arrangement demonstrate the group's ability to create credible alternatives. For India, these are not initiatives targeted at any currency. In any case, India has officially said it's against de-dollarisation or any attempt to target the US currency. It has also ruled out any proposal for a common BRICS currency.BRICS provides India with markets, along with trade diversification, de-risking and supply-chain opportunities. According to a commerce ministry press release, intra-BRICS merchandise trade reached approximately $1.17 trillion in 2024. India exported an estimated $82 billion in goods to BRICS members in FY2025–26, alongside approximately $31.3 billion in services exports in 2024. BRICS membership deepens India’s trade relationships with Russia (energy), Brazil (agriculture/commodities), Gulf and African countries, diversifying away from overreliance on any single partner.The first of course is to forge a consensus on West Asia that would enable a joint BRICS declaration, a task complicated by the presence of the UAE and Iran in the group. India would not like the event to end with a Chair's Statement, like what happened with the foreign ministers' meeting, knowing well that no BRICS summit has concluded without a comprehensive joint declaration. Foreign secretary Vikram Misri said last week India has received cooperation from all members and the government is working to arrive eventually at a constructive outcome that benefits all BRICS stakeholders. India will focus on drafting a resolution rooted in the UN Charter, dialogue and diplomacy, freedom of navigation and civilian protection, while looking to ringfence economic agreements from contentious political issues by acknowledging respective national positions.Balancing relations with the US is another key concern for India, which is hosting the summit fresh off a tariff firestorm with Washington. US President Donald Trump sees the grouping itself as an assault on the US currency and has threatened to impose 100 percent tariffs on BRICS nations if they work to replace the US dollar. India backs legitimate local-currency settlement, while maintaining it is against any common BRICS currency or China-centered replacement mechanism. As it walks the diplomatic tightrope, India must steer initiatives like the integration of central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) but without appearing to endorse any anti-dollar bloc.Another challenge for India is to prevent China's predominance without destabilising its bilateral relations with Beijing. For all the talk about BRICS' combined power, China enjoys a vastly asymmetrical influence with its trade, investment, manufacturing and critical mineral leverage. Wary of China's efforts to advance its own economic interests, India has not endorsed SCO’s 2030 economic roadmap and it must find a way to work with China in BRICS on shared objectives but without allowing the forum to be co-opted as a Chinese economic or geopolitical platform.This also intersects with the challenge of ensuring that an expanded grouping remains governable and cohesive, especially with countries like Pakistan and Bangladesh pursuing membership with support from Beijing. True multipolarity and consensus-driven equality within the organisation are key imperatives for India.As Jaishankar said while announcing India's summit agenda, BRICS must transition now from a forum for discussions to a platform for delivery. In that spirit, India seems focused on delivering an outcome-oriented summit with key deliverables like a unanimous BRICS declaration, logistics supply-chain cooperation framework, incubator/ startup network, development finance, cross-border payment and continued support for Indian priorities like UNSC reforms and counterterrorism.To conclude, inclusion of the African Union was not the only major takeaway from the G20 summit in 2023. Perhaps more dramatic was the last-minute consensus on Ukraine through a compromise language crafted by India, allowing a G20 declaration. India can take confidence from that diplomatic triumph, heading into another tough but potentially rewarding global summit.
Article Summary: India will host the annual brics summit on september 12-13 at bharat mandapam. The theme of india's 2026 chairship is building for resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability. This would be the 18th summit of the grouping that brings together 11 major emerging and developing economies.

Article Title: 'Attack on one is attack on all': Pakistan warns Houthis, invokes Mecca defence pact
Article Text:
Pakistan warns Houthis that its defence alliance with Saudi Arabia and Turkey

Pakistan warned Tuesday that its newly formed defence alliance with Saudi Arabia and Turkiye could be activated if the conflict in Yemen spills into Saudi territory, saying there should be “no ambiguity” that an attack on any one of the three members would be treated as an attack on all.Pakistan’s defence minister Khawaja Asif said the agreement signed by Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye in Makkah last month was defensive in nature and required the three countries to respond if any member came under unprovoked aggression.“There should be no ambiguity; there is no need for any clarity that this is a joint defence agreement,” Asif said in an interview with Geo TV. He added that Pakistan was “bound by the terms and conditions of this pact” and would honour its commitments to Saudi Arabia if required.His comments came hours after Iran-aligned Houthi forces launched a wave of missile and drone attacks on southern Saudi Arabia, targeting cities as well as economic and energy infrastructure. At least 73 civilians were injured, according to the Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen.Asif stressed that the alliance did not give its members a mandate to launch offensive operations against another country on their own initiative.“This is not an aggressive agreement under which the three countries would, on their own initiative, attack another country. But if there is any aggression against one member state, all three member states will respond,” he said.The minister said he was not aware of any contact between Islamabad and Riyadh following the latest Houthi attacks. He also expressed hope that tensions would ease, while warning the Houthis against extending the Yemen conflict into Saudi Arabia.“If they try to export them, the clauses of this agreement to counter aggression will become operative,” Asif said.Pakistan prime minister Shehbaz Sharif separately condemned the Houthi attacks, describing them as “cowardly” and saying they threatened civilian lives as well as regional peace and security. He said Pakistan stood in “unwavering” solidarity with Saudi Arabia and reaffirmed support for the kingdom's sovereignty, security and territorial integrity.The Saudi-led coalition said the attacks had temporarily disrupted operations at some targeted sites, while specialised teams worked to contain fires and secure the facilities. Riyadh also warned against continued attacks on civilians and commercial shipping.The Houthis said the attacks were retaliation for recent Saudi airstrikes on areas of northwestern Yemen under their control. The group had also accused Saudi Arabia of bombing a prison in Al Hazm on Monday, killing at least 11 people.Asif described the Houthis as “non-state actors” and said sympathy for Iran's position in its ongoing conflict with the United States existed across parts of the Muslim world, including Yemen. But he cautioned against allowing those sentiments to widen the conflict.He also said the Mecca alliance could act as a deterrent without necessarily requiring a military response to every attack.“We don't need to respond to a brick with a stone,” Asif said, arguing that the combined military capabilities of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye should themselves serve as a deterrent.
Article Summary: Pakistan warns houthis that its defence alliance with saudi arabia and turkey could be activated if the conflict in yemen spills into saudi territory. Pakistan’s defence minister khawaja asif said the agreement was defensive in nature. He stressed that the alliance did not give its members a mandate to launch offensive operations against another country on their own initiative.
